steps.body:
In `sequences-series` you watched partial sums pile up against a **ceiling** at a/(1 − r), and stop. That was convergence, made visible — and it was the only test you had.

But it works for **one family only**. A geometric series has a fixed ratio. Most series do not.

So the question becomes general: **how would you know whether a pile of partial sums has a ceiling at all?**

widget.prompt: 4 + 4r + 4r² + … Set the ratio so the forever-sum settles on exactly 8 — the ceiling you met in Algebra 2.
widget.successFeedback: r = 0.5, ceiling 8. Now hold on to the PICTURE and let go of the formula: what actually made the sum settle was that the TERMS shrank fast enough. Every test in this chapter is a different way of asking that one question — and the geometric case is just the one where the answer was easy.
widget.lowFeedback: The ceiling is under 8 — the terms shrink too fast, so the pile stops short.
widget.highFeedback: The ceiling is over 8 — the terms shrink too slowly. As r approaches 1 the ceiling escapes altogether.

predict.prompt: The ratio dial starts at r = 0.9. Before you touch it: at that ratio, does the forever-sum's ceiling sit ABOVE the 8 you are aiming for, or BELOW it?

options.label: Above 8
Below 8 — the terms still shrink, so the pile stays small

predict.reveal: Above — far above. At r = 0.9 the terms DO shrink, but too slowly: each keeps 90% of the last, and the ceiling sits at 40, five times the target. As r approaches 1 the ceiling escapes altogether, so you must bring the ratio DOWN to make the sum settle on 8.

cml.actionGoal: Build successive terms and connect recursive pattern, explicit rule, and long-run behavior.

steps.body: The first thing to check, always.
explanationVariants: If the terms do NOT go to zero, the sum cannot settle — you keep adding lumps of a fixed size forever. That is the nth-term test, and it is the cheapest one there is.
It is a one-way test: terms going to zero does NOT guarantee convergence. It only rules out the hopeless cases.

widget.prompt: The terms of a series do not approach 0. What can you conclude?

options.label: It diverges because nonzero-size terms keep forcing finite jumps in the sums
options.feedback: Right, and it is the cheapest check in the subject. Always run it first.

options.label: It converges because repeated terms can cancel each other out
options.feedback: The opposite. If the terms never fade, the partial sums keep taking finite jumps forever and no ceiling can hold them.

options.label: No conclusion follows until a comparison test is chosen
options.feedback: Something very definite can: divergence. It is the CONVERSE that says nothing — terms going to zero does not guarantee convergence.

options.label: It converges when the nonzero terms are all positive
options.feedback: Sign is irrelevant here. Terms that do not fade to zero kill any series, positive or not.

steps.body: The trap in the other direction.
explanationVariants: The harmonic series 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … has terms going to zero and still DIVERGES — the pile grows without bound, just very slowly.
So the nth-term test can only ever prove divergence. It can never prove convergence, and treating it as if it could is the classic error.

widget.prompt: The terms of 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4 + … go to zero. Does the series converge?

options.label: No — the harmonic series diverges, even though its terms fade to nothing.
options.feedback: Right, and it is the single most important counterexample in the subject: fading terms are NECESSARY for convergence but nowhere near sufficient.

options.label: Yes — the terms go to zero, so the sum must settle.
options.feedback: That is the trap. The harmonic series grows without bound; it just takes its time. Its terms fade too slowly to be summable.

options.label: Yes, because it is like a geometric series with r < 1.
options.feedback: It is not geometric at all — the RATIO between consecutive terms is not constant. That is exactly why the old test cannot decide it.

options.label: Only if you add the terms in the right order.
options.feedback: For a series of positive terms the order makes no difference at all. This one diverges however you arrange it.

steps.body:
So every test asks ONE question — *do the terms fade fast enough?* — in a different way:

**nth-term** — do they fade at all?
**comparison** — at least as fast as something you know?
**ratio** — does each term shrink by a factor that settles below 1?
**alternating** — do they fade AND flip sign?

Each is a different way of getting a ceiling over the pile.
The ratio test IS the geometric idea.
explanationVariants: The ratio test asks what |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| settles down to. If that limit is under 1, the tail behaves like a geometric series with that ratio — and geometric series with r < 1 converge.
It is the old test, freed from the requirement that the ratio be the SAME every time. It only has to settle.

widget.prompt: Why does the ratio test work?

options.label: A settled ratio below 1 makes the tail shrink like a convergent geometric series
options.feedback: Right. It is the geometric test with the requirement loosened: the ratio no longer has to be CONSTANT, only to settle.

options.label: Every series has one fixed geometric ratio after enough terms
options.feedback: Very few are. The point is that the TAIL behaves geometrically once the ratio has settled, which is enough to build a ceiling over the pile.

options.label: Terms approaching zero alone force any series to converge
options.feedback: The harmonic series has terms going to zero and diverges. The ratio test asks something stronger: how FAST they shrink.

options.label: It applies only when every term is positive and decreasing
options.feedback: It uses ABSOLUTE values precisely so that signs cannot interfere. It works for any series.

steps.body: Which test, and what does it say?
hints: Look at the terms of Σ n/(n + 1): 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, 4/5, …
What are they heading toward? Not zero — they climb toward 1.
So the cheapest test settles it immediately.
explanationVariants: The terms n/(n + 1) tend to 1, not 0. So by the nth-term test the series DIVERGES — you are adding roughly 1 forever.
Never reach for a clever test before running the cheap one. Half of these questions die at the first line.

options.label: No—the terms approach 1 rather than 0, so the nth-term test says diverge
options.feedback: Right, and it took one line. Always run the cheap test first.

options.label: Yes—the terms stay below 1, so their total can settle
options.feedback: Being less than 1 is not enough; they must FADE TO ZERO. These climb toward 1, so you are adding roughly 1 forever.

options.label: Yes—the ratio eventually drops below 1 and proves convergence
options.feedback: The ratio here settles at exactly 1, which is the inconclusive case — and in any case the nth-term test has already killed it.

options.label: It depends on where the series starts, because early terms control the sum
options.feedback: Convergence is a question about the TAIL, and no starting point can rescue terms that do not fade.

takeaways: The geometric ceiling was one test for one family. Every other test is a different way of getting a ceiling over the pile.
nth-term test: if the terms do not fade to zero, it diverges. It can NEVER prove convergence.
The harmonic series is the standing counterexample: terms fade to zero, and it diverges anyway.
steps.teaser: Next: use a series to BUILD a function — and watch the polynomial hug the curve.

concept.body: Before any clever test, ask the cheap question: **do the terms go to zero?** If they do not, the series diverges and you are finished. If they do, you have learned nothing yet — and now the real work starts.

explanationVariants: The terms of Σ (2n)/(n + 5) head toward 2, not 0, so the series diverges.

widget.prompt: The terms of a series tend to 2. Does it converge?

options.label: No — it diverges.
options.feedback: Right: you are adding roughly 2 forever, and no ceiling can hold that.

options.label: Yes, if 2 is small enough.
options.feedback: Size is irrelevant. Any nonzero limit means the pile keeps taking finite jumps forever.
